title: Brand Stories · Episode 2
chapters: IKEA and the genius of the flat pack
New Coke: the taste test that backfired
The Tylenol murders and the art of crisis response

units.t: Brand Stories. Episode two.
In this episode: IKEA and the genius of the flat pack, New Coke: the taste test that backfired, The Tylenol murders and the art of crisis response and Kodak and the innovator's dilemma.
Part one. IKEA and the genius of the flat pack.
A teenager selling pens by mail order in rural Sweden built the world's biggest furniture retailer.
The secret involved taking the legs off a table.
A teenager in Småland.
Ingvar Kamprad grew up on a farm called Elmtaryd near the village of Agunnaryd, in Småland, a region of southern Sweden known for poor, stony soil and thrifty people.
As a boy he sold matches, then seeds, Christmas cards and pencils.
In 1943, aged seventeen, he registered his own company.
He named it by combining his initials with the first letters of his farm and village: Ingvar Kamprad, Elmtaryd, Agunnaryd, or IKEA.
At first it sold pens, wallets and picture frames by mail order.
In the late 1940s Kamprad added furniture made by local manufacturers, and before long furniture was the main business.
Legs off, costs down.
In the 1950s IKEA employee Gillis Lundgren was trying to fit a table into a car after a photo shoot.
It would not go in, so he took the legs off.
The company realised that flat-packed furniture is cheaper to store and ship and less likely to be damaged, and customers could carry it home and assemble it with simple tools.
Flat packing was not entirely new, but IKEA made it the heart of its business.
Lundgren went on to design many products, including the Billy bookcase in 1979.
Thrift is built into the strategy.
Designers often start with a target price and work backwards, choosing materials, shapes and packaging to save money.
A bookcase that packs a few centimetres flatter means more fit on a truck.
The boycott that backfired.
IKEA's low prices made established Swedish furniture retailers furious.
In the 1950s they pressured local manufacturers to stop supplying the upstart, and IKEA was even barred from some furniture trade fairs.
Rather than give in, Kamprad looked further afield.
In the early 1960s IKEA began having furniture made in Poland, where production costs were much lower.
The boycott, meant to crush the company, pushed it to build its own international supply chain and design more of its own products.
That made IKEA cheaper still and gave it control over how its furniture was made and packed.
It is a classic case of turning a threat into an advantage by changing the approach rather than the goal.
The customer does the work.
IKEA's first store opened in Älmhult in 1958, and the model has been refined ever since.
It rests on a simple bargain: the customer does part of the work and pays a lower price.
In a traditional shop, staff fetched items, delivered them and assembled them.
At IKEA, shoppers browse a showroom, note product codes, collect flat boxes from a self-serve warehouse, take them home and build the furniture themselves.
Even the winding one-way path through the showroom is designed to show customers as much of the range as possible.
Restaurants, play areas and cheap snacks encourage families to stay longer, and longer visits tend to mean bigger purchases.
Today IKEA has hundreds of stores in dozens of countries, including several in Australia.
The IKEA effect.
Assembling furniture can be frustrating, but it may also make people like it more.
In a study published in 2012, researchers Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely asked people to assemble simple IKEA storage boxes, fold origami or build Lego models.
Those who had built the item were willing to pay noticeably more for it than people offered an identical item already assembled.
The researchers called this the IKEA effect: labour leads to love.
When participants failed to finish building something, the effect faded.
Businesses use the idea widely, from build-your-own toy shops to apps that let you customise your profile.
The key idea: Ingvar Kamprad founded IKEA at seventeen, and the name comes from his initials and his home.
Part two. New Coke: the taste test that backfired.
In 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its famous recipe with one that beat the old drink in blind taste tests.
Within three months the company was begging forgiveness.
Winning the blind test.
By the early 1980s Coca-Cola's share of the American soft drink market had been sliding for years while Pepsi gained.
Pepsi targeted younger drinkers and, from 1975, ran the Pepsi Challenge: shoppers sipped from two unmarked cups, and on camera they often picked Pepsi.
Coca-Cola's own blind tests gave the same uncomfortable answer.
Under chief executive Roberto Goizueta, the company did the unthinkable and reformulated a recipe treated as almost sacred for nearly a century.
In the secret Project Kansas, it put a sweeter, smoother cola through about 200,000 taste tests.
It beat both old Coke and Pepsi.
On 23 April 1985, Coca-Cola announced that the old formula was retired.
The backlash.
The reaction caught the company off guard.
Phone lines at its Atlanta headquarters were flooded with thousands of angry calls, and sacks of letters arrived from people who felt betrayed.
Some customers stockpiled cases of the original.
In Seattle, Gay Mullins started the Old Cola Drinkers of America and won wide media coverage.
Comedians and columnists piled on.
Much of the anger was not about flavour at all.
Many complainers had never compared the two drinks carefully.
They were upset that something tied to childhood, family and national identity had been taken away without anyone asking them first.
What the research missed.
The flaw in the research is easy to see in hindsight.
Blind tests asked a narrow question: which liquid do you prefer right now, in a small sip?
They never asked how people would feel if the old drink disappeared for good.
One popular explanation is that sweeter drinks tend to win quick sip tests even when people would not choose them for a whole can, though how much that mattered here is still argued about.
Some of the company's own focus groups hinted at trouble, as a minority reacted angrily to the idea of losing the original, but the strength of that feeling was underestimated.
Customers buy meaning and habit as well as features.
Classic returns.
By early July the company had seen enough.
On 11 July 1985, 79 days after the launch, it announced the original formula would return as Coca-Cola Classic, and the news led television bulletins across the country.

Company president Donald Keough told reporters that some critics would say Coca-Cola had made a marketing mistake, some cynics would say it had planned the whole thing, and the truth was that it was not that dumb and not that smart.
For a while both drinks were sold side by side.
Classic comfortably outsold its replacement.
New Coke was later renamed Coke II and lingered in a few markets for years before quietly disappearing.
Lessons that lasted.
Was New Coke a disaster?
In the short term it was an embarrassment, but there is an odd twist.
The uproar reminded Americans how attached they were to the original, and after Classic returned, Coca-Cola's sales recovered and its lead over Pepsi strengthened.
The company did not plan this.
It did one thing well: once it understood its mistake, it reversed quickly and publicly instead of defending the decision for years.
Business schools still teach the case.
Data can be precise and still answer the wrong question.
Loyal customers can feel ownership of a product they do not legally own.
And humility, shown early, is often cheaper than stubbornness.
The key idea: Coca-Cola changed its recipe because blind taste tests, including its own, showed people preferred sweeter drinks.
Part three. The Tylenol murders and the art of crisis response.
In 1982 seven people in Chicago died after taking poisoned painkillers.
How one company responded became the textbook example of handling a crisis.
Seven deaths in Chicago.
On 29 September 1982 a twelve-year-old girl in a Chicago suburb took an Extra-Strength Tylenol capsule for a cold and died within hours.
Over the next few days six more people in the Chicago area died the same way, including three members of one family.
Investigators found the link: capsules of Tylenol, the best-selling painkiller in the United States, had been filled with potassium cyanide.
The bottles had come from different factories, which suggested the poison was not added during manufacturing.
Someone appeared to have taken bottles from shops, tampered with them and returned them to the shelves.
Panic spread across the country, and copycat tampering incidents followed.
The expensive choice.
Tylenol was made by McNeil Consumer Products, a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson, and held roughly a third of the American market for over-the-counter painkillers.
Almost overnight that share collapsed, reportedly to under ten per cent.
Experts predicted the brand would never recover, and some advised retiring the name.
The company had not caused the crime, and the tampering seemed limited to one region.
A narrow, legalistic response would have been cheaper.
Led by chairman James Burke, it chose the expensive path.
It worked with police, regulators and the media, warned the public not to take any Tylenol capsules, and recalled around 31 million bottles nationwide at a cost of about 100 million US dollars.
Burke said the company's credo, written in the 1940s and putting customers first, guided its decisions.
Fixing the packaging.
The company did not stop at the recall.
Within about two months it relaunched Tylenol capsules in triple-sealed packaging: a glued box, a plastic seal around the neck and a foil seal over the mouth of the bottle.
These did not make tampering impossible, but they made it much easier to see.
Sales representatives visited doctors and pharmacists, and discount coupons helped win customers back.
In 1983 the United States passed a federal law making tampering with consumer products a crime, and tamper-evident seals spread across food, drink and medicine.
The foil seal you peel off a new jar today is partly a legacy of the 1982 poisonings.
A mystery never solved.
The criminal side never found closure.
A man named James Lewis sent Johnson and Johnson a letter demanding one million dollars to stop the killings.
He was convicted of extortion and spent years in prison, but he was never charged with the poisonings and always denied them.
He died in 2023.
Investigators reopened the case several times and tested new evidence as forensic science improved, yet the murders remain officially unsolved.
For the families, that means decades without answers.
For business, it is a reminder that some crises begin entirely outside a company's control.
The only thing it truly controls is how it responds.
What it teaches.
Within about a year Tylenol had regained much of its lost market share, a recovery few experts thought possible.
The case is still taught as a model of crisis management, although some scholars note the company was helped by being an obvious victim rather than a culprit.
Several principles stand out.
Act fast, even before you have every fact.
Put public safety ahead of short-term profit, and be seen doing so.
Communicate openly with authorities and the media rather than hiding.
Fix the underlying weakness so the problem cannot easily happen again.
Companies that later stumbled in a crisis were often criticised for doing the opposite: delaying, minimising and protecting themselves first.
The key idea: In 1982 someone laced Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules with cyanide and returned them to shop shelves.
Part four. Kodak and the innovator's dilemma.
In 1975 a young Kodak engineer built the world's first digital camera.
Nearly four decades later, Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
How does a company invent the future and still lose it?
Selling the film.
In the 1880s George Eastman set out to make photography simple enough for anyone.
His first Kodak camera came loaded with film; when the roll was finished you posted the whole camera back, and the company developed the pictures and returned it reloaded.
The slogan was You press the button, we do the rest.
Kodak became a household name, and for much of the twentieth century dominated the US film market.
At its peak in the late 1980s it employed more than 140,000 people worldwide.
Its model resembles razors and blades.
Cameras sold cheaply, while the real money came from film, chemicals, paper and processing.
Margins were high, but the whole company, from factories to managers' bonuses, was built around chemistry.
Anything that threatened film threatened its profits.
The camera nobody wanted.
In 1975 Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a prototype digital camera.
It was about the size of a toaster, weighed several kilograms and took around 23 seconds to record a single black and white image, at about 0.
01 megapixels, onto a cassette tape.
Viewing it required a special playback system and a television.
Sasson later recalled that managers found it interesting but were unsure why anyone would want to look at photos on a TV.
That reaction was reasonable at the time, as the technology was crude and expensive.
The problem was what happened over the following decades, as digital improved rapidly while Kodak's core business still depended on film.
The innovator's dilemma.
In 1997 Harvard professor Clayton Christensen published The Innovator's Dilemma.
Studying industries such as computer disk drives, he saw a pattern.
Well-run companies listened to their best customers and improved existing products.
New technologies usually began worse, cheaper and aimed at small or unfashionable markets.
Sensible managers ignored them, since they offered lower profits and the main customers did not want them.
But the new technology kept improving until it was good enough for everyone, and by then the old leaders were too far behind.
Christensen called this disruption.
The painful insight is that leaders did not fail through stupidity.
They failed by doing what good managers are trained to do.
Too little, too late.
Kodak was not blind to digital.
It invested heavily, held valuable patents and for a time was one of the leading sellers of digital cameras in the United States.
But digital cameras were a competitive hardware business with thin margins, nothing like the steady profits of film.
Then smartphones made separate cameras unnecessary for most people.
Photos were shared online rather than printed, so the processing business shrank too.
Kodak cut tens of thousands of jobs and sold divisions, but filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States in January 2012.
It later emerged as a much smaller company focused on commercial printing and other specialised areas.
Another road, and a warning.
Japan's Fujifilm faced the same collapse in film sales yet survived far better.
Its leaders asked what else the company was good at.
Making film involves sophisticated chemistry, including handling collagen and preventing fading from oxidation.
Fujifilm applied it to medical imaging, pharmaceuticals, specialised materials and skincare, and bought other businesses to speed the change.
Both companies saw digital coming; the difference lay partly in how willing each was to treat its old core business as temporary.
The pattern repeats.
Blockbuster reportedly had the chance to buy a young Netflix around 2000 and declined, then filed for bankruptcy in 2010.
A useful question: is there a cheaper, simpler product experts dismiss as not good enough, but which keeps improving each year?
The key idea: Kodak made photography easy, but its profits came mostly from film and processing that every photo needed.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does Kamprad's early life suggest about IKEA's roots?
Answer. Thrift and small-scale selling from youth.
Question two. Why did Coca-Cola decide to change its recipe?
Answer. Blind tests showed many people preferred sweeter rivals.
Question three. What suggested the poison was not added at the factory?
Answer. Affected bottles came from different factories.
Question four. Why was Kodak's business built around film rather than cameras?
Answer. Film and processing were bought again and again.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
